# Preparing Real-World Data

::: {.callout-note title="Connection with the theoretical volume"}
The mathematical representation of data and the foundations of probability and statistics are developed in greater depth in Chapters 1, 2, and 3 of *Mathematical Foundations of Machine Learning* [@rodriguez2026fundamentos].
:::

## Chapter objectives

By the end of this chapter, the reader will be able to:

- identify the provenance of a dataset and document its transformations;
- locate and download the ATUS dataset from the official INEGI portal;
- organize original files, processed files, and educational samples within a project;
- read, inspect, select, and transform variables in R;
- construct response variables for classification;
- save prepared datasets for later chapters;
- distinguish official source data from author-derived products;
- recognize important data limitations before fitting a model.

## Introduction

In professional practice, data rarely arrive ready for a machine-learning algorithm. Before modeling, it is necessary to understand where the data came from, inspect their structure, identify missing values and special codes, transform variables, and document every relevant decision.

This book uses two applied routes based on Mexican open data:

1. **ATUS**, published by INEGI, as the main thread for mobility and road-safety problems;
2. **COVID-19 historical open data**, published by Mexico's Ministry of Health, as a transversal case for preparation, classification, and evaluation in a public-health context [@salud_covid_historicos_2022].

::: {.callout-important title="Provenance and derived products"}
The original files belong to the institutions that publish them. Processed datasets, educational samples, derived variables, graphics, models, and interpretations in this book are academic products prepared by the author. They are not official institutional results and do not imply endorsement by the data providers.
:::

## Recommended data organization

To preserve traceability and reproducibility, original sources should be separated from the products generated during the analysis.

```text
libro-machine-learning-r/
├── datos/
│   ├── atus_2024.csv
│   └── covid19/
│       ├── originales/
│       ├── procesados/
│       ├── muestras/
│       └── diccionarios/
├── _quarto.yml
└── referencias.bib
```

This structure helps answer three essential questions: **where did the data come from, what transformations were applied, and which file should be used to reproduce a particular example?**

# Applied Case A: ATUS

## Downloading ATUS from INEGI

This book uses the **Road Traffic Accidents in Urban and Suburban Areas (ATUS)** statistical dataset published by Mexico's National Institute of Statistics and Geography, INEGI [@inegi_atus_2024].

To reproduce the examples in this edition:

1. open the official ATUS portal: <https://www.inegi.org.mx/programas/accidentes/>;
2. locate the open-data section;
3. select **2024**;
4. download and, when necessary, decompress the file;
5. identify the annual CSV file;
6. save it inside the `datos` directory as `atus_2024.csv`.

::: {.callout-tip title="Using another year"}
Another period can be used, but the year must be documented and the variable names and categories must be checked against the corresponding data dictionary before reusing the chapter code.
:::

## How to cite the data

INEGI's free-use terms require acknowledgment of the source [@inegi_terminos_libre_uso]. When the data have been processed by the author, an appropriate source note is:

> **Source:** Author's processing of INEGI data, Road Traffic Accidents in Urban and Suburban Areas (ATUS), 2024.

## Load the required packages

```{r load-packages-data-preparation}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)
source("../util_graficas.R")
```

## Locate and read the ATUS file

```{r locate-read-atus}
atus_files <- list.files(
  path = "../datos",
  pattern = "^atus.*\\.csv$",
  full.names = TRUE,
  ignore.case = TRUE
)

raw_files <- atus_files[
  !grepl("ml_preparado", basename(atus_files), ignore.case = TRUE)
]

if (length(atus_files) == 0) {
  stop(
    paste(
      "No ATUS CSV file was found in the datos directory.",
      "Download it from the official INEGI portal."
    )
  )
}

atus_path <- if (length(raw_files) > 0) {
  raw_files[1]
} else {
  atus_files[1]
}

atus <- read_csv(
  atus_path,
  show_col_types = FALSE,
  locale = locale(encoding = "UTF-8")
)

message("File read: ", atus_path)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Code explanation"}
The code first looks for an original ATUS file. If one is not present in the repository, the prepared dataset can be used as a rendering fallback. That fallback makes the book reproducible online, but it does not replace the complete preparation process from the original INEGI file.
:::

## Inspect structure and variable names

```{r inspect-atus}
data.frame(
  rows = nrow(atus),
  columns = ncol(atus)
)

head(atus)

names(atus) <- toupper(names(atus))
names(atus)
```

## Select variables of interest

```{r select-variables-atus}
variables_of_interest <- c(
  "ANIO", "MES", "ID_ENTIDAD", "ID_MUNICIPIO",
  "ID_HORA", "ID_DIA", "DIASEMANA", "TIPACCID",
  "CAUSAACCI", "CLASACC"
)

existing_variables <- intersect(variables_of_interest, names(atus))
missing_variables <- setdiff(variables_of_interest, names(atus))

atus_base <- atus |>
  select(all_of(existing_variables))

existing_variables
missing_variables
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Check the data dictionary"}
If a variable is missing, it should not be replaced by another variable merely because its name looks similar. First consult the data dictionary and metadata for the specific ATUS edition being used.
:::

## Construct the response variable

The first classification problem distinguishes **accidents involving casualties** from **accidents involving property damage only**.

```{r create-response-atus}
if ("CLASACC" %in% names(atus_base)) {
  atus_model <- atus_base |>
    mutate(
      CLASACC_TXT = str_to_lower(as.character(CLASACC)),
      accidente_con_victimas = case_when(
        str_detect(CLASACC_TXT, "sólo daños") ~ "Solo daños",
        str_detect(CLASACC_TXT, "solo daños") ~ "Solo daños",
        str_detect(CLASACC_TXT, "daños") ~ "Solo daños",
        str_detect(CLASACC_TXT, "no fatal") ~ "Con víctimas",
        str_detect(CLASACC_TXT, "fatal") ~ "Con víctimas",
        TRUE ~ NA_character_
      )
    ) |>
    filter(!is.na(accidente_con_victimas))

} else if ("ACCIDENTE_CON_VICTIMAS" %in% names(atus)) {
  atus_model <- atus |>
    transmute(
      MES,
      ID_HORA,
      DIASEMANA,
      TIPACCID,
      CAUSAACCI,
      accidente_con_victimas = as.character(ACCIDENTE_CON_VICTIMAS)
    ) |>
    mutate(
      accidente_con_victimas = case_when(
        str_to_lower(accidente_con_victimas) %in% c("con víctimas", "con victimas") ~ "Con víctimas",
        str_to_lower(accidente_con_victimas) %in% c("solo daños", "sólo daños") ~ "Solo daños",
        TRUE ~ NA_character_
      )
    ) |>
    filter(!is.na(accidente_con_victimas))

  message(
    "A prepared ATUS dataset was used as a rendering fallback. ",
    "Use the original INEGI file to reproduce the preparation from scratch."
  )
} else {
  stop("Neither CLASACC nor ACCIDENTE_CON_VICTIMAS was found. Check the data dictionary.")
}

table(atus_model$accidente_con_victimas)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Why are the category labels kept in Spanish in the code?"}
The prepared ATUS file is shared by both language editions of the book and is also used by later chapters and Colab notebooks. Keeping the stored factor labels unchanged avoids creating two incompatible versions of the same analytical dataset. The surrounding explanations and graphical labels can still be presented in English.
:::

## Prepare and save the ATUS modeling dataset

```{r prepare-save-atus}
atus_ml <- atus_model |>
  mutate(
    MES = as.factor(MES),
    ID_HORA = as.character(ID_HORA),
    DIASEMANA = as.factor(DIASEMANA),
    TIPACCID = as.factor(TIPACCID),
    CAUSAACCI = as.factor(CAUSAACCI),
    accidente_con_victimas = factor(
      accidente_con_victimas,
      levels = c("Con víctimas", "Solo daños")
    )
  ) |>
  select(
    accidente_con_victimas,
    MES,
    ID_HORA,
    DIASEMANA,
    TIPACCID,
    CAUSAACCI
  ) |>
  na.omit()

# In the English project the shared data directory is one level above.
# The following write is disabled during rendering to avoid modifying source data.
# write_csv(atus_ml, "../datos/atus_ml_preparado.csv")

data.frame(
  rows = nrow(atus_ml),
  columns = ncol(atus_ml)
)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Reproducible writing step"}
When reproducing the workflow locally from the original ATUS file, remove the comment marker from `write_csv()` to save the prepared dataset. During book rendering, the repository's validated prepared file is left unchanged.
:::

# Applied Case B: COVID-19

## Selecting the analysis period

The 2026 edition compares the historical closures available for **2020 through 2025**, using the same confirmed-case criterion and the year of symptom onset whenever the structure of the files permits a comparable definition.

The comparison table stored with the book is:

```text
datos/covid19/procesados/conteo_casos_confirmados_2020_2025.csv
```

```{r covid-period-comparison}
covid_counts <- read_csv(
  "../datos/covid19/procesados/conteo_casos_confirmados_2020_2025.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

covid_counts
```

In the validated comparison currently included with this edition, **2022 contains the largest number of confirmed records among the periods processed under a homologated scheme**. The 2024 and 2025 rows are explicitly marked as non-homologated and therefore are not used to select the modeling period.

::: {.callout-important title="Do not confuse publication year with epidemiological period"}
The year of a historical closure file should not automatically be interpreted as the year of symptom onset. The preparation workflow uses `FECHA_SINTOMAS` when that variable is available and comparable across closures.
:::

## Select the prepared dataset reproducibly

```{r covid-locate-prepared}
selected_year <- covid_counts |>
  filter(
    ESTADO == "PROCESADO",
    !is.na(CASOS_CONFIRMADOS)
  ) |>
  slice_max(
    order_by = CASOS_CONFIRMADOS,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) |>
  pull(ANIO)

covid_path <- file.path(
  "../datos/covid19/procesados",
  paste0("covid19_mexico_", selected_year, "_ml_preparado.csv.gz")
)

if (!file.exists(covid_path)) {
  stop(
    paste(
      "The prepared COVID-19 dataset selected by the comparison table was not found:",
      covid_path
    )
  )
}

message("Selected COVID-19 dataset: ", covid_path)
message("Selected year: ", selected_year)
```

## Read and inspect the prepared dataset

```{r covid-read-prepared}
covid <- read_csv(
  covid_path,
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

dim(covid)
names(covid)
```

## Binary variables and special codes

In the prepared dataset, binary clinical variables are recoded for teaching purposes as:

| Value | Interpretation |
|---:|---|
| 0 | No |
| 1 | Yes |
| `NA` | Unspecified, ignored, or not applicable according to the original catalog |

`TIPO_PACIENTE` is represented as 0 = outpatient and 1 = hospitalized. The variable `MURIO` is derived from the presence of a valid death date in `FECHA_DEF` and is used only as an administrative outcome for the educational exercises in this book.

::: {.callout-warning title="Clinical interpretation"}
`MURIO` does not turn the exercise into a clinical prediction model. The underlying administrative records may contain selection bias, unknown values, changes in surveillance practices, and differences in coverage. The models in this book are educational and must not be used for diagnosis, treatment, or individual medical decisions.
:::

## Review missing values

```{r covid-missing-values}
missing_covid <- covid |>
  summarise(
    across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))
  ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "missing"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(missing))

head(missing_covid, 10)
```

## Number of comorbidities

`NUM_COMORBILIDADES` summarizes, when available, diabetes, COPD, asthma, immunosuppression, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, obesity, chronic kidney disease, and smoking.

```{r covid-comorbidities}
covid |>
  count(NUM_COMORBILIDADES) |>
  arrange(NUM_COMORBILIDADES)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Educational samples and prevalence"}
If a stratified sample is used to facilitate classification exercises, the proportion of deaths in that sample **must not be interpreted as prevalence or as a population mortality rate**. Probabilistic models trained on samples whose class prevalence has been intentionally modified should not be interpreted as calibrated population probabilities without an additional calibration or weighting procedure.
:::

## Data-preparation checklist

Before moving to model fitting, verify that:

- the source and period are documented;
- a separate copy of the original source files is preserved;
- every variable used in the analysis exists in the corresponding data dictionary;
- special codes are handled explicitly;
- derived variables are documented;
- processed datasets are not presented as unmodified official data;
- tables and graphics acknowledge the data source;
- educational samples are not interpreted as population estimates.

## Interactive laboratory: preparing data

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
Use this laboratory to explore the effect of missing values, mean or median imputation, and standardization on a small synthetic environmental dataset.

```{shinylive-r}
#| standalone: true
#| viewerHeight: 760
#| components: [viewer]

library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Interactive data preparation"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      sliderInput(
        "missing_pct",
        "Percentage of missing values",
        min = 0,
        max = 40,
        value = 15,
        step = 5
      ),
      selectInput(
        "imputation",
        "Imputation method",
        choices = c("Mean" = "mean", "Median" = "median")
      ),
      checkboxInput(
        "scale_vars",
        "Standardize variables",
        value = TRUE
      ),
      numericInput(
        "seed",
        "Random seed",
        value = 123,
        min = 1
      )
    ),
    mainPanel(
      h4("Data with missing values"),
      tableOutput("raw_table"),
      h4("Prepared data"),
      tableOutput("prepared_table"),
      h4("Preparation summary"),
      tableOutput("summary_table")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  raw_data <- reactive({
    set.seed(input$seed)

    d <- data.frame(
      temperature = round(rnorm(12, 25, 4), 1),
      humidity = round(rnorm(12, 55, 12), 1),
      pollution = round(rnorm(12, 40, 10), 1)
    )

    n_missing <- round(length(as.matrix(d)) * input$missing_pct / 100)

    if (n_missing > 0) {
      m <- as.matrix(d)
      missing_positions <- sample(seq_len(length(m)), n_missing)
      m[missing_positions] <- NA
      d <- as.data.frame(m)
    }

    d
  })

  prepared_data <- reactive({
    d <- raw_data()

    for (j in seq_along(d)) {
      replacement <- if (input$imputation == "mean") {
        mean(d[[j]], na.rm = TRUE)
      } else {
        median(d[[j]], na.rm = TRUE)
      }

      d[[j]][is.na(d[[j]])] <- replacement
    }

    if (isTRUE(input$scale_vars)) {
      d <- as.data.frame(scale(d))
    }

    d
  })

  output$raw_table <- renderTable({
    raw_data()
  }, digits = 2)

  output$prepared_table <- renderTable({
    prepared_data()
  }, digits = 3)

  output$summary_table <- renderTable({
    before <- raw_data()
    after <- prepared_data()

    data.frame(
      Measure = c(
        "Missing cells before preparation",
        "Missing cells after preparation",
        "Imputation method",
        "Standardization"
      ),
      Value = c(
        sum(is.na(before)),
        sum(is.na(after)),
        ifelse(input$imputation == "mean", "Mean", "Median"),
        ifelse(input$scale_vars, "Yes", "No")
      )
    )
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
```
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
### Laboratory available in the web edition
The interactive version allows the reader to change the percentage of missing observations, compare mean and median imputation, and turn variable standardization on or off.
:::

## Chapter summary

Reliable machine learning begins before model fitting. Data provenance, variable definitions, missing values, transformations, class construction, sampling, and limitations must all be documented. The ATUS and COVID-19 routes in this chapter establish the reproducible datasets that will be reused throughout the following modeling chapters.
